passages: [prose] Information on lifespan was found for 54 ant species (Table 1) and 10 termite species (Table 2). The most striking pattern emerging from these Tables is the very long lifespan of queens, with values higher than 20 years in some species. An inspection of Tables 1 and 2 reveals that most data come from queens reared in the laboratory, typically with only few colonies studied. Hence, these lifespan estimates should be regarded as approximate and only reflect lifespan under laboratory conditions. For some species the maximum lifespan is underestimated because the queen died from the lack of water, escaped from the colony, or simply was still alive at the time of publication. Insufficient information was given for most of species to determine whether more than one colony had been followed in the laboratory and to assess the average lifespan of queens. Field data are also not without problems in most cases. For example, when the lifespan of queens is based on the lifespan of colonies it may be that some queens are replaced thus increasing colony longevity and the presumed queen lifespan. Queen replacement has indeed been recently shown to occur in monogyne colonies of the fire ant Solenopsis invicta (DeHeer and Tschinkel, 1998).

[prose] Comparative studies are increasingly used to identify factors responsible for the evolution of plant and animal phenotypes and social insects provide ideal systems for such studies as a result of their modular growth and their bewildering diversity in social organization. Here I review data on the lifespan of queens in ants and termites because such data are highly relevant for comparative analyses on life-history. Lifespan has been reported in 53 ant and 10 termite species. Information on the mode of colony founding and number of queens per colony is also provided for the 53 ant species. Finally, I suggest that students of social insects would greatly benefit if information on colony characteristics, individual phenotypes and behaviour would become available for a larger number of species, perhaps on a database that would be accessible on the web.

[prose] The aim of the present paper is to make available information on the lifespan of ant and termite queens that I collected from the literature and unpublished observations by colleagues. The primary aim was to test evolutionary theories on ageing by investigating whether the evolution of eusociality had been paralleled by an increase in queen lifespan [the expected pattern if lifespan is influenced by extrinsic mortality (Alexander et al., 1991; Keller and Genoud, 1997)]. Unfortunately, space limitation prevented us from providing detailed information on queen lifespans and the relevant references. The publication of the full data set should be particularly useful because data for several species come from unpublished observations or papers published in French. As data on queen number (monogyne versus polygyne) and mode of colony founding were also collected for our analysis I also provide these data and the relevant references. These informations on queen lifespan and social organization are based on an extensive literature research and the personal observations of many colleagues.

[prose] I encountered several problems while classifying species as monogyne or polygyne. In most cases species were categorized without any indication of the number of colonies surveyed or the number of queens found per nest. It is becoming increasingly clear that species that always have only one queen per colony and species that always have multiple queens per colony are only endpoints on a monogyny-polygyny continuum. Most species probably form both single and multiple queen colonies. Hence, species should better be classified on a monogyny-polygyny continuum with either the proportion of polygyne colonies or the average queen number per colony as a measure of the “level” of polygyny. Unfortunately, such information is available for only a minority of the species. An additional problem is that the number of queens per colony may vary among seasons, as for example has been reported in the Argentine ant (Keller et al., 1989) and species of the genus Leptothorax (Herbers and Stuart, 1996; J. Heinze, pers. comm.).
